questions.stem: Several classes each take a random sample of 40 students from the same school and calculate the mean height of their sample. Why do their sample means differ?
options: Different samples contain different students, so sample means vary
Some of the classes must have measured incorrectly
The population mean changes each time a sample is taken
Sample means can only take whole-number values
questions.explanation: A sample mean depends on which individuals are chosen, so it varies from sample to sample: it is a random variable. The population mean stays fixed; only the estimates of it change.

questions.stem: What kind of random variable is the sample mean of a measured quantity such as mass?
options: A fixed number, not a random variable
questions.explanation: Sample means of measurements can take any value in an interval, so they are treated as continuous random variables. They are not fixed numbers, because they change from sample to sample.

questions.stem: A population has standard deviation 18. For random samples of size 81, the sample means are approximately normal with mean μ and standard deviation:
questions.explanation: The standard deviation of the sample mean is σ/√n = 18/√81 = 18/9 = 2. Dividing by n = 81 instead of √81 gives about 0.22, and 18 is the spread of single values.

questions.stem: A population has standard deviation 18. For random samples of 81, about 95% of sample means lie within what distance of the population mean?
questions.explanation: The sample means have standard deviation 18/√81 = 2, and about 95% lie within two standard deviations, that is within 4 of μ. The value 36 uses σ instead of σ/√n.

questions.stem: Why can a single sample mean x̄ not tell us the exact value of the population mean μ?
options: The sample mean is always smaller than μ
μ can only be found from a sample of size 30
Another sample would give a different value of x̄
questions.explanation: Because x̄ varies from sample to sample, it is only a guide to μ. An interval estimate around x̄ expresses how far from μ it might be.

questions.stem: Which value of z is used for a 95% confidence interval for μ?
questions.explanation: For 95% confidence, Pr(−z ≤ Z ≤ z) = 0.95, so Pr(Z ≤ z) = 0.975 and z ≈ 1.960. The value 1.645 is for 90%, and 2.326 for 98%.

questions.stem: Which value of z gives a 90% confidence interval for μ?
questions.explanation: The middle 90% leaves 5% in each tail, so z satisfies Pr(Z ≤ z) = 0.95, giving z ≈ 1.645. Using Pr(Z ≤ z) = 0.90 gives 1.282, which puts all 10% in one tail.

questions.stem: Which value of z gives a 98% confidence interval for μ?
questions.explanation: The middle 98% leaves 1% in each tail, so Pr(Z ≤ z) = 0.99 and z ≈ 2.326. Solving Pr(Z ≤ z) = 0.98 gives 2.054, a slip that leaves 2% in one tail; 2.576 is for 99%.

questions.stem: An approximate 68% confidence interval for μ uses which value of z?
questions.explanation: About 68% of a normal distribution lies within one standard deviation of the mean, so z = 1 gives an approximate 68% interval. About 95% lies within two standard deviations.

questions.stem: A random sample of 100 has x̄ = 52.4, from a population with σ = 8. Find the 95% confidence interval for μ, to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The margin is 1.96 × 8/√100 = 1.568, giving 50.83 ≤ μ ≤ 53.97. Leaving out √n gives the far wider 36.72 to 68.08, and z = 1.645 gives the 90% interval.

questions.stem: A random sample of 36 bags has mean mass 18.5 kg and standard deviation 4.2 kg. Using s for σ, find the 90% confidence interval for μ, to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The margin is 1.645 × 4.2/√36 = 1.645 × 0.7 ≈ 1.15, giving 17.35 to 19.65. Using z = 1.96 gives the 95% interval, z = 2.326 gives the 98% interval, and 15.68 to 21.32 divides s by √6 instead of √36.

questions.stem: A random sample of 225 apples has mean diameter 6.8 cm and standard deviation 1.5 cm. Using s for σ, find the 98% confidence interval for μ, to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: σ/√n = 1.5/15 = 0.1 and the margin is 2.326 × 0.1 ≈ 0.23, giving 6.57 to 7.03. The interval 6.60 to 7.00 uses z = 1.96 (95%), and 6.59 to 7.01 uses the slip z = 2.054.

questions.stem: A random sample of 64 has s = 12. Find the margin of error for a 95% confidence interval for μ.
questions.explanation: The margin of error is z × s/√n = 1.96 × 12/8 = 2.94. Using z = 1.645 gives the 90% margin 2.47, and dividing by n = 64 gives 0.37.

questions.stem: A confidence interval for μ is 41.3 ≤ μ ≤ 44.7. What are the sample mean and the margin of error?
questions.explanation: The sample mean is the midpoint, (41.3 + 44.7)/2 = 43.0, and the margin is half the width, 3.4/2 = 1.7. The full width, 3.4, is twice the margin.

questions.stem: A 95% confidence interval for μ from a sample of 49 is 41.3 ≤ μ ≤ 44.7. Find the sample standard deviation used, to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The margin is 1.7, so 1.96 × s/7 = 1.7 and s = 1.7 × 7/1.96 ≈ 6.07. Using z = 1.645 gives 7.23, and using the full width 3.4 instead of the margin gives 12.14.

questions.stem: A researcher wants a 95% confidence interval for μ with a margin of error of at most 0.5, and estimates σ as 4. What is the smallest sample size needed?
questions.explanation: Solve 1.96 × 4/√n ≤ 0.5: √n ≥ 15.68, so n ≥ 245.86, and n must be rounded up to 246. Rounding down to 245 gives a margin just above 0.5.

questions.stem: What is the smallest sample size giving a 90% confidence interval for μ with margin of error at most 2, if σ = 15?
questions.explanation: Solve 1.645 × 15/√n ≤ 2: n ≥ (1.645 × 15/2)² ≈ 152.2, so n = 153. Using z = 1.96 gives 217, which is the 95% requirement.

questions.stem: With σ = 10 and n = 25, what is the width of the 95% confidence interval for μ?
questions.explanation: The margin is 1.96 × 10/5 = 3.92, and the interval runs from x̄ − 3.92 to x̄ + 3.92, so its width is 7.84. The margin alone is half the width.

questions.stem: A random sample of 36 has x̄ = 30, from a population with σ = 6. Find an approximate 68% confidence interval for μ.
questions.explanation: With z = 1, the interval is 30 ± 6/√36 = 30 ± 1. Using σ instead of σ/√n gives 24 to 36, and 28 to 32 uses z = 2, the approximate 95% interval.

questions.stem: A 95% confidence interval for μ is 20.0 ≤ μ ≤ 24.0. Using the same sample, find the 90% confidence interval, to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The 95% margin is 2, so σ/√n = 2/1.96 ≈ 1.020. The 90% margin is 1.645 × 1.020 ≈ 1.68, giving 20.32 to 23.68. Taking σ/√n as 2 gives 18.71 to 25.29, wider than the 95% interval, which cannot be right; 19.63 to 24.37 uses z = 2.326, the 98% value.

questions.stem: A random sample of 36 has x̄ = 12 and s = 3. Using z = 2, find an approximate 95% confidence interval for μ.
questions.explanation: s/√n = 3/6 = 0.5, and 2 × 0.5 = 1, giving 11 to 13. Using s alone gives 6 to 18, and 11.5 to 12.5 forgets to multiply by z.

questions.stem: If the confidence level is raised from 90% to 98% with the same sample, the confidence interval becomes:
options: centred on a different sample mean
questions.explanation: A higher confidence level needs a larger z (2.326 instead of 1.645), so the margin of error grows. The centre stays at the same x̄.

questions.stem: With the same s and confidence level, how does multiplying the sample size by 4 change the margin of error?
questions.explanation: The margin is z × s/√n, and √(4n) = 2√n, so the margin halves. To quarter it, the sample size would need to be 16 times larger.

questions.stem: A survey of 50 people gave a margin of error E. With the same s and confidence level, how many people are needed for a margin of error of E/2?
questions.explanation: Halving the margin needs √n to double, so n must be multiplied by 4: 4 × 50 = 200. Doubling n to 100 reduces the margin only by a factor of √2.

questions.stem: Two samples of the same size give 95% confidence intervals for μ. Sample A has s = 5 and sample B has s = 9. Which is true?
options: Both intervals have the same width
B gives the narrower interval because its spread is larger
questions.explanation: The margin z × s/√n is proportional to s, so the sample with more variation gives a wider interval. Sample size and confidence level are the same, so only s differs.

questions.stem: Sample A has n = 100 and s = 20. Sample B has n = 400 and s = 30. Which gives the narrower 95% confidence interval for μ?
questions.explanation: A has margin 1.96 × 20/10 = 3.92 and B has 1.96 × 30/20 = 2.94, so sample B gives the narrower interval despite its larger s. The larger sample more than makes up for the extra spread.

questions.stem: From one sample, a 90% and a 98% confidence interval for μ are calculated. Which statement is correct?
options: The two intervals have different centres
The two intervals do not overlap
questions.explanation: Both are centred on the same x̄, and the 98% interval has the larger margin, so it contains the 90% interval. Only the value of z differs.

questions.stem: A researcher wants a narrower confidence interval for μ but cannot collect any more data. What could be changed, and at what cost?
options: Use σ/n in place of σ/√n, so the interval is narrower
Use a z value of 0, so the interval has no width
Lower the confidence level, so fewer such intervals contain μ
Raise the confidence level, so more such intervals contain μ
questions.explanation: A lower confidence level uses a smaller z and so a narrower interval, but a smaller proportion of such intervals capture μ. Changing the formula would give a wrong interval, not a better one.

questions.stem: What does "95% confidence" mean for a confidence interval for μ?
options: About 95% of intervals built this way from repeated samples contain μ
μ lies in this particular interval 95% of the time
95% of the population values lie in the interval
questions.explanation: The confidence level describes the method: across many samples, about 95% of the intervals capture the fixed μ. Any one calculated interval either contains μ or does not.

questions.stem: A researcher calculates the 95% confidence interval 50.8 ≤ μ ≤ 54.0. Which statement is correct?
options: 95% of individual values are between 50.8 and 54.0
This interval either contains μ or it does not
There is a 95% probability that μ is between 50.8 and 54.0
questions.explanation: Once the interval is calculated, μ is a fixed number that is inside it or not; the 95% refers to how often the method succeeds. The interval estimates μ, not the spread of individual values.

questions.stem: Forty different random samples are used to calculate forty 90% confidence intervals for the same μ. How many of them would be expected NOT to contain μ?
questions.explanation: About 90% of such intervals contain μ, so about 10% of 40, that is 4, would miss it. The value 36 is the number expected to contain μ.

questions.stem: Which statement about confidence intervals for μ is correct?
options: Not every confidence interval contains μ
A confidence interval always contains every sample mean
questions.explanation: However high the confidence level, some samples give an interval that misses μ. A 98% interval misses μ for about 2% of samples.

questions.stem: A manufacturer claims its batteries last 55 hours on average. A 95% confidence interval from a sample is 50.8 ≤ μ ≤ 54.0. What can be concluded?
options: The claim is supported because 55 is close to 54.0
The claim is doubtful, but the interval does not prove it false
questions.explanation: Since 55 is outside the interval, the sample suggests the mean is lower than claimed. A confidence interval is only a guide, so a definite statement is not possible.

questions.stem: A school claims its students sleep 8.5 hours a night on average. A 90% confidence interval from a sample is 8.1 ≤ μ ≤ 8.7. What can be concluded?
options: The claim is proved true, since 8.5 is in the interval
The claim is proved false, since 8.5 is not the midpoint
The true mean must be exactly 8.4, the interval midpoint
The data are consistent with the claim, but do not prove it
questions.explanation: The claimed value lies inside the interval, so the sample gives no reason to doubt it. Other values in the interval are equally consistent with the data, so the claim is not proved.

questions.stem: A random sample of 100 has x̄ = 100 and s = 10. The 90% interval is 98.36 ≤ μ ≤ 101.64 and the 98% interval is 97.67 ≤ μ ≤ 102.33. How do the intervals relate to a claim that μ = 98?
options: 98 is inside the 90% interval but outside the 98% interval
98 is outside the 90% interval but inside the 98% interval
questions.explanation: The claimed value lies below 98.36 but above 97.67. So the 90% interval casts doubt on the claim while the 98% interval does not, which shows why conclusions are a guide only.

questions.stem: When is it reasonable to use the sample standard deviation s in place of σ in a confidence interval for μ?
options: Whenever the population is exactly normal
When σ is unknown and the sample is sufficiently large
Only when the sample size is less than 10
Only when s is larger than σ
questions.explanation: If σ is unknown, s from a sufficiently large sample is a good approximation to it. Small samples give unreliable values of s.
